articles.headline: INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.
articles.text:
We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views, representing the most interesting events of the range cattle industry. There are thirty-six well-executed photographs in the series, making an extremely interesting and realistic panorama of cowboy life. We will sell the complete set for $5 or,

THE COW BOY A YEAR AND THE SET, $6

This offer will probably be recalled soon, but the bargain can now be secured by calling on or addressing THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy offers its remaining sets of thirty-six Huffman round-up photographs for $5, or with a year's subscription for $6.

articles.text: The Canadian Blood Indians are crossing the line to give battle to their old enemies, the Gros Ventres. Military forces both from the United States and Canada are hastening to the scene and will put a stop to the proceedings.
articles.summary: Canadian Blood Indians were reported crossing the line to fight the Gros Ventres, with U.S. and Canadian troops on their way.

articles.text: Newspapers have, since the surrender of Geronimo and Natchez to Gen. Miles, used up columns of abuse on the General for his alleged lenient terms to his prisoners. It now transpires that the Apaches surrendered unconditionally and can be punished by any authority the government sees fit to recognize.
articles.summary: The paper notes it now appears the Apaches under Geronimo and Natchez surrendered unconditionally to Gen. Miles.

articles.text: Spearfish had a fire Sunday that completely burned out about a third of the business portion of the town. Beginning at "Uncle Jimmy" Rogers' hotel it swept everything on the block facing Main street, to and including Williams' boot and shoe store. The total loss is about $75,000. We think Spearfish has sufficient recuperative power to recover from the loss and it will then be of the same benefit that the Chicago fire was to Chicago.
articles.summary: A Sunday fire burned about a third of Spearfish's business district, with losses of about $75,000.

articles.text: Governor Pierce's annual report to the secretary of the Interior is a carefully worded document in which he deals with facts and wisely avoids any further opening of the division question. He says that the debt of the territory is $568,200; not half the amount authorized by Congress limiting the debt to be contracted by the territories. This fact makes the territorial bonds as good securities as can be found in the market. He estimates the increase in population this year at 85,000. The report ends with an earnest appeal for admission as Dakota does and has for a long time posessed all the requirements for state-hood.
articles.summary: Editorial approving Governor Pierce's annual report, which puts the territorial debt at $568,200, estimates population growth of 85,000 and appeals for statehood.

articles.text: Trouble began last Monday over the attempted return by the Chicago pork packers to the ten-hour-a-day rule. All the pork butchers at the Stock Yards have struck except in one or two houses and in sympathy with them, many of the beef butchers have also quit work. The strike is so far, the most orderly that has been conducted. A special committee appointed by Master Workman Powderly is now in Chicago and a speedy and peaceful settlement of the difficulty is expected. The proprietors very reasonably urge that they cannot pay ten hours' wages for eight hours' work when they come in direct opposition with Kansas City and St. Louis houses paying the same wages for ten hours' work.
articles.summary: Chicago pork butchers struck over the packers' return to the ten-hour day; the paper sides with the packers.

articles.text: At the Morton county Republican convention held Tuesday, delegates were elected to the legislative convention favorable to T. J. Mitchell of Mandan. The fight was between Mitchell and Lyon and was won by Mitchell after a sharp contest. The fight was still further complicated by the nomination at the same time of a full set of county officers. F. A. Briggs was nominated for treasurer, B. J. VanVleck for register of deeds, F. E. Bowen for district attorney, Geo. Harmon for sheriff and H. P. Hillis for auditor. It is hardly possible now to tell how the nomination will turn out at the legislative convention. The west Missouri country will be given a member of the lower house and the fight will again be between Lyon and Mitchell, with chances about even.
articles.summary: The Morton county Republican convention chose legislative delegates favoring T. J. Mitchell over Lyon and nominated county officers.

articles.text: There seems but little doubt now that the seven Chicago anarchists will hang. The judge has denied their motion for a new trial and the supreme court, if appealed to, will undoubtedly back up the decision of the lower court. The summing-up of the judge in the case was a wonderfully clear statement of the facts and proved beyond a doubt the correctness of the decision. He quoted a long list of articles from the anarchists' written and spoken words that showed conclusively that for three years they had openly advocated killing the police and prominent men. The murders at the Haymarket last May were the legitimate out-come of their articles and were undoubtedly incited by them. Whether they or any of them threw the bomb that killed the policemen matters not. Judge Gary clearly showed that they advocated the use of dynamite; had set the day when it would be used; and that it was used as fore-told and fore-advised. If seven miscreants ever deserved hanging it is the seven who will assuredly suffer that fate soon in Chicago.
articles.summary: Editorial applauding Judge Gary's denial of a new trial for the seven Chicago anarchists.

articles.text: Stock Inspector Fred Willard returned Monday night from Oliver county, where he had been quarantining Etheringtons' herd of cattle. Dr. Halloway, assistant territorial veterinarian of Montana, returned on the same train. The Dr. pronounces that the disease is undoubtedly pleuro-pneumonia. A long trench eight feet deep was dug on the ground where the herd had been quarantined and yesterday every animal in the herd, whether showing symptoms of the disease or not, was shot and thrown into the trench. One hundred barrels of lime were then thrown on the carcasses and they were then buried deeply. There never was a more perfect case of the complete stamping out of a disease and stockmen are congratulated on their escape from what threatened to be a vital danger. The disease was located a long way from the range country but if one animal had strayed away from the infected herd it might in the course of time have spread the disease here. The Montana Stockgrowers' Association, through Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt two Dakota members of the executive committee, are to be thanked for the prompt action taken.
articles.summary: Stock Inspector Fred Willard and Montana's Dr. Halloway confirmed pleuro-pneumonia in the Etherington herd in Oliver county, which was shot and buried in lime; the Montana Stockgrowers' Association, through de Mores and Roosevelt, is credited with the prompt action.

articles.text: It is at last learned that "Bobby" Adams, one of the most notorious and successful burglars in the world, robbed the Minneapolis post-office of the $15,000 worth of stamps recently. He has been arrested and will doubtless be convicted as the evidence is said to be conclusive.
articles.summary: Burglar "Bobby" Adams has been arrested for the $15,000 Minneapolis post-office stamp robbery.

articles.headline: More of the Butchers' Advocate.
articles.text:
We have several times had occasion to refer to the Butchers' Advocate of New York and its attacks on western dressed beef.

The Advocate was started as the organ of New York retail butchers and for the expression of their opposition to western dressed beef. No one denies the right of any corporation or set of individuals to establish a newspaper to represent them in all their interests and to lawfully oppose anything detrimental to those interests. The establishment of the Advocate for these reasons was not only right but was a good move on the part of the New York butchers.

But there is a limit to the lawful opposition of the Advocate in its crusade against western dressed beef and that limit it has not only reached but passed. No untruthful statements are lawful in backing up a position no matter how right that position may be.

In its last issue, the Advocate step-father's the report that pleuro-pneumonia has broken out near Medora and insinuates strongly that the diseased cattle were killed here and sent to New York to be sold in the Co.'s retail shops.

If the above were the truth in either of its parts, the Advocate or any sensible man knows that the Co. would be criminally liable in a large amount. If they were liable, the Advocate would be the first to take steps to have the Co. punished. No such steps have been or will be taken, because the Advocate knows the statement to be untrue. The nearest the disease has come to Medora is 160 miles away. The infected cattle were immediately quarantined and have now not only been killed but buried in a trench eight feet deep and the carcasses covered with lime and dirt. And this work was done by money guaranteed by Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt. The former is the head of the Company which the Advocate intimates slaughtered the diseased cattle for their retail trade and the latter is one of the prominent raisers of the "sage-stubble" beef, whom the Advocate accuses of selling diseased carcasses to confiding eastern purchasers. This article will reach the eye of the editor of the Advocate and we call upon him to right the wrong he has done range interests by stating that pleuro-pneumonia had broken out near Medora. The infected district is as far practically from Medora as is Australia. Over 160 miles of farming country lie between, across which the disease could scarcely have passed and certainly never will now that every animal in the infected herd whether diseased or not has been killed and buried.

The Advocate has a way of denying articles by saying that they are the work of the Co. That it cannot resort to such subterfuge in answering this article we will say that we have had no word of correspondence in any form with any member of the firm directly or indirectly on the subject; that we are in no sense in their pay and that we are now and for some time have been paying them more for rent alone than we have been receiving from them.

The facts as to the location of the disease are easily learned and a manly retraction from the editor of the Advocate is the only course left open for him.
articles.summary: Editorial denying the New York Butchers' Advocate's charge that pleuro-pneumonia broke out near Medora and that diseased cattle were sold by de Mores' company, noting the infected herd 160 miles away was destroyed with money guaranteed by de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt.

articles.headline: Forage Plants of the West.
articles.text:
WASHINGTON, Sept. 13.—Commissioner Coleman, of the Agricultural Department some time ago sent Professor George Vasey, the botanist of the department, to make an investigation of the grasses of the arid region of the west, in accordance with an appropriation for that purpose, to ascertain if there were other native grasses and forage plants which would probably be more productive than those now prevailing in that region. Vasey has just returned from his trip, and having made a very thorough investigation of the country included in northeastern New Mexico, eastern Colorado, western Kansas, and western Nebraska, is full of interesting information on the subject.

He says: The native grasses occupying this great tract are numerous, but those which constitute the great [proportion?] of the vegetation, and are the main [reliance?] for the support of stock, are but two kinds, namely, gramma grass and buffalo grass. These are botanically of different genera, but by the greater part of the people are both called buffalo grass. They are grasses of low growth, forming patches of greater or less extent, having spaces of bare soil between the patches. The leaves are very short and much crowded close to the ground. When not too closely cropped by cattle slender, flowering stems are sent up in July and August bearing at the summit one or two short banner-like spikes, which are rather conspicuous, as they stand out horizontally, and are swayed by the breeze. The true buffalo grass (buchloe dactyloides) formed extensive cushion-like beds, covering the ground closely with its short compact foliage, which is of a lighter green color than the gramma. Thess two grasses, in varying proportions, constitute generally 60 per cent of all the grass product. In most localities the gramma grass is much the more abundant of the two. There are several other kinds, which in some localities form a considerable amount of forage. One of these is the Colorado blue-stem or blue grass, very different from the

BLUE GRASS OF THE EAST.

This is a great reliance for stock in winter, and often cut and cured for hay.

Another frequent grass is the blue-joint of Kansas and Nebraska, botanically a species of audropojon. It grows with rather a tall, coarse stock and long leaves, and although somewhat coarse is a valuable grass and everywhere cut for hay. In the bottom lands and in alkaline soils a grass prevails which is called alkali or salt grass. It often forms extensive beds, with the appearance of Kentucky blue grass, and is eaten by horses and cattle, and is said to be nutritious. There can be no doubt that the gramma and buffalo grasses have a very high nutritious value, but they grow so sparsely that cattle require an extensive range in order to obtain proper support. When we come to inquire as to the number of cattle that can be supported on a square mile or on a quarter section we shall realize that there is great poverty as to the amount of grass.

There is a surprising difference in the estimates as to the supporting ability of the plains of these States, some stating that it requires forty or fifty acres to support one animal, others giving twenty to thirty, and still others ten to fifteen acres. All these estimates are correct as to certain localities, and over the entire region it may be considered probable that the average amount required would be about fifteen acres to the head. The inquiry will naturally arise, can not the grazing capacity of this region be greatly increased by substituting more productive grasses?

The results of Professor Vasey's investigations on this subject show that this may undoubtedly be done. So long as the old system of keeping cattle on ranches of vast extent, without providing winter feed or shelter, continued no improvement could be expected, for

NO CHANGE CAN BE EFFECTED

without cultivation of the land. But the cattlemen have mostly evacuated Kansas, and are rapidly removing their herds from Nebraska to occupy Wyoming and Montana, and the vacated lands are now being rapidly occupied for homesteads by incoming settlers, notwithstanding the risks to be encountered from scarcity of water and possible droughts. From the results of farming experiments in various sections during a few years past very sanguine expectations are entertained as to the value of the land for general farming purposes. Admitting the possibility of moderate success in that line, there can yet be no doubt that the country is naturally a pastoral one, and that it can by proper means in the future be made to sustain a much greater number of cattle and sheep than it has in the past. This will be done by holders of limited quantities of land, from a quarter section up to a section or more, who will provide fodder for their stock in the winter and give them suitable shelter, and at the same time break up their land and lay down pastures of new and more productive grasses. What these grasses shall be is yet an open question, and can only be settled by carefully-conducted experiments. It is highly desirable that the government should establish a central and characteristic location, an experimental grass station, where all the commonly cultivated grasses and forage plants and also the more promising native ones could be thoroughly tried under various conditions of culture, and the results given to the public. Undoubtedly a properly conducted and well continued series of experiments in this direction would result in important discoveries of great value to the future residents in this arid district.—[Inter Ocean.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Inter Ocean on botanist George Vasey's survey of western range grasses, arguing for smaller fenced holdings, winter feed and a government experimental grass station.

articles.text: Sylvane Ferris was called on last Friday to mourn the death of his favorite horse, "Water-skip." He hung himself by jumping into an adjoining manger to the one in which he was hitched in Jos. Ferris' stable.
articles.summary: Sylvane Ferris's favorite horse "Water-skip" died last Friday after hanging itself in a manger in Joe Ferris' stable.

articles.text: Herman Dickman writes us from Chicago that he is clerking in a store there, is married and has a daughter. He thinks there is no place like the Bad Lands and intends visiting here if he can get a vacation. George Myers called on him on his way home to Ohio.
articles.summary: Herman Dickman writes from Chicago that he is clerking, married with a daughter, and hopes to visit; George Myers called on him on his way to Ohio.

articles.text: A. C. Huidekoper's statement while here, that he was sure natural gas could be obtained by boring for it in the Bad Lands, has had a half-confirmation by the striking of a good vein of the gas at Fargo. The formation and physical characteristics of the Bad Lands point more conclusively than do any other part of Dakota, to the existence of natural gas.
articles.summary: A gas strike at Fargo is taken as partial confirmation of A. C. Huidekoper's belief that natural gas lies under the Bad Lands.

articles.text: It seems that some kind of disease is attacking the deer, as four dead ones were found near together about two miles south of town, without a mark on them to indicate the cause of their death. One of them was the pet deer belonging to Mr. Eeger. W. F. VanDriesche has written to a competent authority to learn if possible the cause of their death.
articles.summary: Four dead deer, including Mr. Eeger's pet, were found unmarked two miles south of town; W. F. VanDriesche has written for expert advice.
